div.p: When depression has not improved enough after at least two antidepressants taken at an adequate dose for an adequate length of time, it may be treatment-resistant depression (TRD). Symptoms such as persistent sadness, low energy, and loss of interest can continue to affect everyday life.
A U.S. study estimated that approximately one-third of adults receiving medication for major depression had treatment-resistant depression.
Our team reviews each patient's symptoms and treatment history to build a personalized plan that may include novel therapies, medication management, and psychotherapy.

Before TMS and Potential response after TMS brain visualization

div.p: What it is and how it works: A noninvasive treatment that uses magnetic pulses to stimulate brain networks involved in mood and OCD. FDA-cleared for depression and as an additional treatment for OCD.
Potential benefits: May reduce persistent depression symptoms. An OCD-specific treatment protocol may reduce obsessive thoughts and compulsive behaviors.
What it is and how it works: An FDA-approved prescription nasal spray for adults with treatment-resistant depression. It acts on NMDA receptors in the brain's glutamate system.
Potential benefits: May reduce depression symptoms, with improvement observed as early as approximately 24 hours in clinical trials. It can be used with or without an oral antidepressant for TRD.

img.alt: Official Spravato Logo and Nasal Spray Applicator
Adult patient resting comfortably in a chair with an eye mask

div.p: What it is and how it works: Low-dose ketamine delivered through an IV. It acts on NMDA receptors in the brain's glutamate system and is used off-label for depression.
Potential benefits: May relieve depression symptoms within hours for some patients when standard treatments have not provided enough relief. Additional treatments may be needed to maintain benefits.

div.div: *In a 2021 U.S. study, an estimated 30.9% of adults with medication-treated major depression had treatment-resistant depression. Source: Zhdanava et al., Journal of Clinical Psychiatry. 2021;82(2):20m13699.
